articles.description:
The CAPA that taught me what an email isn't
Two years ago I inherited a CAPA queue that included a finding from our prior notified body audit. The wording was polite but unambiguous: "The approval records for the post-market surveillance report could not be verified against a Part 11-compliant system." I went looking. The approval record was a four-message email thread. The approver had typed their name in a reply. The original report was an attachment that had since been edited and re-uploaded to the shared drive. The "signature" and the "record" had no binding I could demonstrate to an auditor — or to myself.
That's the trap. "Approve by email" feels rigorous. Someone wrote a name. Someone replied "approved." There's a date. It looks like evidence. Under 21 CFR Part 11, it isn't.
When an…
articles.title: 21 CFR Part 11 is where 'approve by email' shops quietly fail — a typed name is not a signature

Here's a bug I've shipped more than once: tests pass locally, demo looks great,
seed data with foreign keys that don't actually


  
  
  The quiet problem with hand-rolled seed data


Say you've got the classic Prisma setup:
model User {
  id    Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  email String @unique
  posts Post[]
}

model Post {
  id       String @id @default(uuid())
  title    String
  author   User   @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id])
  authorId Int
}

When you fake seed data for Post, what goes in authorId? If you're using a
looks fine in a
A JOIN between Post and User returns rows that shouldn't exist, or none at all.
A real FK constraint in Postgres rejects the insert outright (violates foreign key constraint).
Any UI that renders "post by author" either crashes or shows ghosts.
Your seed data passed the eyeball test and failed the only test that matters:
faker (and the dozens of wrappers around it) are great at generating values —
relationships. They'll
authorId: 8471 on a post when no user 8471 exists, because they
To generate honest relational data you need to:
Generate the parent rows first (User), and remember their real ids.
Generate the child rows (Post), and set each authorId to an id that was
actually generated for a user.
It's not hard conceptually — it's just annoying to do by hand every single time
I got tired of writing this glue, so I built a small VS Code extension,
SeedForge,
schema.prisma and generates the data for you. The free
It's also on Open VSX if you're
Even if you never touch SeedForge: next time you write seed data, ask whether
JOINs will finally tell
What's your approach to relational test data — hand-written factories, SQL
fixtures, something else? Genuinely curious what's working for people.
articles.title: Your seed data is lying to you — the case for foreign-key-consistent test data

articles.description:
Short answer: use a background job queue for outbound media webhook work, make every receiver idempotent, and reserve cron for scheduled enqueueing. The queue may deliver a standard message more than once; the design is correct only when the same logical delivery can be processed twice without producing two customer-visible effects.
This is a governance decision, not a search for an “exactly once” checkbox. A media SaaS sending asset.ready, caption.updated, and license.expiring notifications across US and EU deployments has three different records in play: the application owns the event, the queue owns pending work, and the destination owns the effect. Confusing those records is how a retry policy turns into duplicate publication notices.
Adopt the queue-and-worker design only with stable …
articles.title: 4 Governance Rules for a Simple Node.js SaaS App Background Job Queue

articles.author: 江流石
articles.description:
When you point Claude Code or Codex at a third-party relay and it errors, read the status code first — it tells you exactly what's wrong:
404 — wrong address. Usually the /v1 on base_url: Anthropic-compatible endpoints have no /v1 (Claude Code appends /v1/messages); OpenAI-compatible endpoints need /v1.
401 / 403 — auth failed. Key copied in full? Credit left? Model id in the station's list? Claude Code must use ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (Bearer), not ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
429 — the station is rate-limiting. Switch stations or wait; retrying just lengthens the queue.
400 / content blocked — upstream moderation. Retry in plain English/Chinese; if it keeps firing, switch stations.
Keep a couple of stations registered so a single one rate-limiting never blocks you. List with tested dates: AI relay station list
Signup links carry my referral param; strip ?aff= if you prefer.
articles.title: Debugging a relay API in Claude Code / Codex: 401 vs 404 vs 429
